item.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a concrete pathway for using early fault‑tolerant quantum computers to simulate nonlinear fluid flows by marrying sparse‑identified reduced‑order models with Walsh‑based Koopman‑von Neumann transport, showing that the per‑step gate count grows only polylogarithmically with spatial resolution. By providing realistic surface‑code resource estimates—about 560 k physical qubits and under two hours for a cylinder‑wake benchmark—it moves quantum simulation from abstract algorithmic proposals toward hardware‑compatible workloads. The work builds on recent advances in quantum PDE solvers and error‑mitigated experiments, suggesting that practical, high‑fidelity nonlinear dynamics could become one of the first near‑term applications where quantum advantage is measurable. However, the projected runtimes still depend on large qubit counts and efficient noise mitigation, so further hardware improvements will be needed before routine deployment.

Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

item.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first experimental teleportation of logical qubits using lattice‑surgery on a superconducting processor with 41 physical qubits, demonstrating that surface‑code patches can be merged and split while preserving encoded information. By showing how repeated stabilizer measurements restore fault tolerance and improve fidelity, it connects directly to recent efforts by Google, IBM and academic groups to build scalable error‑corrected architectures. The ability to move logical states without physically shuttling qubits paves the way for modular quantum processors, although the distance‑three code still leaves room for higher fidelities before full fault‑tolerant operation is achieved.

Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the fault‑tolerance advantage of logical encoding in fusion‑based photonic quantum computers can evaporate when realistic photon‑distinguishability errors are included, highlighting a hidden vulnerability of otherwise promising architectures. By contrasting all‑photonic and emitter‑assisted repeat‑until‑success schemes, the authors demonstrate that the choice of resource‑state generation method can be as decisive for error thresholds as the encoding itself—a nuance that recent photonic hardware roadmaps have largely overlooked. The findings urge experimental teams to prioritize indistinguishability control and to reassess performance projections that assume idealized resource states before scaling up FBQC platforms.

Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.

item.title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces PRISM, a compiler that postpones the choice of a logical‑gate’s physical realization until routing has identified a layout that can execute it, thereby turning a long‑standing phase‑ordering bottleneck into an optimization opportunity for dual‑rail cavity qubits. By keeping multiple loss‑admissible realizations open and selecting the most routing‑friendly one on the fly, PRISM cuts SWAP overhead by roughly 20–30 % and shrinks circuit depth by about 9 %, directly translating into fewer photon‑loss events and up to a 44 % reduction in required repeat attempts. The work demonstrates how hardware‑aware compilation can deliver tangible performance gains for photonic platforms, complementing recent efforts in error‑corrected logical encoding while still being scoped to dual‑rail architectures.

Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

item.title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes measurement‑device‑independent QKD toward real‑world deployment by rigorously handling source flaws and finite‑size effects with a variable‑length security proof based on the marginal‑constrained entropy accumulation theorem. By showing that secret keys can be distilled from as few as 30 000 pulses—even over asymmetric, 80‑km horizontal links—the work bridges the gap between laboratory demonstrations and the longer distances required for commercial satellite constellations. The conic‑optimization framework also offers a practical tool for system designers to fine‑tune transmitter amplitudes and mitigate channel imbalance, though its performance still assumes ideal atmospheric conditions that must be addressed in future field trials.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.

item.title: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a long‑standing open problem by proving that for any finite‑energy multimode Gaussian state the entanglement of formation, its Gaussian variant and the operational entanglement cost all coincide, giving a single, strongly superadditive figure of merit that also lower‑bounds non‑Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. By extending the result to multimode Gaussian channels, the authors obtain exact formulas for both the entanglement cost and the classical capacity under realistic energy constraints, showing that pure Gaussian inputs with simple displacement modulation are already optimal—a finding that streamlines design of continuous‑variable quantum communication systems such as CV‑QKD networks. The work builds on recent advances in bosonic channel capacity theory and resource‑theoretic approaches, while its applicability is limited to finite‑energy regimes, leaving the infinite‑energy idealizations for future study.

Gaussian states and operations are central to continuous-variable quantum information and communication. For systems with any finite number of modes, we prove that entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state. Their common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds entanglement of formation and entanglement cost for arbitrary non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. We then determine the entanglement cost of every multimode Gaussian channel as well as its classical capacity under a mean energy constraint. These quantities reduce to Gaussian covariance optimizations, and the capacity is attained by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation, independently across channel uses. The proof combines geodesic convexity of entanglement for pure Gaussian states with a relative-entropy inequality for arbitrary states. We also obtain a closed formula for the entanglement cost of a family of four-mode bound entangled states.

item.title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that sparse quantum prolate diagonalization can slash the number of required circuit executions from linear to logarithmic in the autocorrelation‑function samples while preserving chemical‑accuracy, a breakthrough for near‑term quantum chemistry on noisy hardware. By leveraging compressed sensing on Quantinuum’s Helios trapped‑ion processor, the authors achieve chemically accurate energies for an embedded arginine–tryptophan pair using circuits with up to 448 two‑qubit gates, showing that sophisticated algorithmic sparsity can offset hardware limitations. If the approach scales as suggested in weakly correlated regimes, it could dramatically accelerate realistic molecular simulations on larger ion‑trap or superconducting devices, though its performance on strongly correlated systems remains an open question.

We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

item.title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that simply adding more layers to a VQE does not guarantee better results – the authors observe a sharp “collapse” of fidelity at intermediate depths before the performance recovers, a double‑descent pattern that stems from optimization failure rather than expressibility limits. By introducing a chained warm‑start strategy they can largely suppress the collapse, yet even then the circuit stalls at modest fidelities despite low energy errors, highlighting that energy alone is an insufficient metric for assessing VQE quality on frustrated spin systems. The findings underscore the need for smarter initialization and multi‑objective diagnostics (fidelity, entropy, total spin) as the community pushes variational algorithms toward larger, more complex problems.

Increasing circuit depth is expected to improve a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We show that this expectation can fail, and that curing the failure does not guarantee the exact ground state. We study a symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates, started from the Néel state, on the frustrated spin-$1/2$ $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg ring with $N=10$ and $12$ sites. With random initialization the fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin change abruptly at intermediate depth ($L\approx 9$ for $N=10$, $L=10$--$12$ for $N=12$), giving improvement, degradation and recovery, a double-descent-like shape. The circuit family is nested and the gradient stays finite, so this is an optimization failure, not a loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. A chained warm start, which extends an optimized shallow circuit with identity layers, removes the collapse and improves energy error and fidelity almost monotonically for most frustration values. However, near $J_2/J_1=0.60$ ($N=10$) and over $J_2/J_1=0.60$--$1.00$ ($N=12$) the warm start stalls at a fidelity of $\approx 0.50$--$0.58$, although the energy error is small and the total spin stays in the $S=0$ sector. Removing the non-monotonic depth dependence is therefore not the same as reaching the ground state, and low energy and a singlet-like state are not sufficient: the fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. The conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.

item.title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article establishes the first unconditional trade‑off between circuit size and entanglement width for symmetric quantum circuits, showing that any polynomial‑size family that respects graph symmetries must generate nearly linear‑scale multipartite entanglement to solve a simple classically easy graph property. By adapting classical pebble‑game lower bounds through a novel quantum indistinguishability theorem, the work clarifies why symmetry alone does not give a free computational shortcut in the quantum regime and highlights entanglement as the critical resource that must be supplied by hardware. The complementary upper bound—showing that unrestricted symmetric circuits can capture all of BQP—helps delineate exactly where design constraints such as limited qubit connectivity or low‑entanglement architectures will hit fundamental limits.

Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

item.title: Quantum Codes for Distributed Quantum Fault Sensing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that carefully designed quantum‑code states can dramatically boost the ability to pinpoint a faulty qubit in a large modular processor, achieving up to a 50 % improvement over naïve independent probes without any protected ancilla memory. By proving a precise criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing and quantifying how much entanglement depth actually helps, it bridges recent advances in quantum error‑correcting codes with the practical need for fast, reliable diagnostics in scalable hardware. The results suggest that modestly sized entangled probe groups—rather than full‑scale Bell pairs—can deliver near‑optimal detection while keeping overheads realistic, a key step toward fault‑tolerant modular architectures. Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying the component affected by a fault. Independent qubits can monitor faults through repeated preparation and measurement. Bell-pair probes improve the guaranteed correct-site probability for unknown local channels, but require partners kept away from the fault. Can entanglement among exposed probes supply this advantage without protected storage? We establish a quantum-code criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing of one unknown local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, suitable code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement, and entanglement depth at most four cannot exceed 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum without protected ancillas also requires a number of probes proportional to the array size to participate in larger entangled factors. For a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background of fixed strength 0 < eta < 1, independent probes already attain the optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling at fixed success between zero and one and a positive false-alarm budget. In three 1000-site comparisons with specified readouts, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, while storing no protected qubits.

Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.

Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first exact, many‑copy formulas for entanglement‑distillable rates and CHSH violations in a deliberately engineered non‑Hermitian two‑qubit model that mimics realistic dephasing and circuit noise. By showing that correlated PPT catalysts cannot boost Bell‑pair yields and providing closed‑form magic‑state concentration probabilities, it bridges abstract resource‑theory results with the practical limits faced by near‑term superconducting or trapped‑ion hardware. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. item.title: Experimental simulation of a Hilbert-space inner-product change
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first experimental demonstration of a controllable change in a qubit’s Hilbert‑space inner product, moving beyond earlier PT‑symmetric simulations that kept the metric fixed and opening a new route for probing non‑Hermitian physics on quantum hardware. By implementing the IP‑change channel with both a qutrit encoding and a two‑qubit Stinespring dilation, and by establishing a rigorous fidelity threshold that excludes trivial mixtures of unitaries, the work shows how subtle metric transformations can be verified even in noisy superconducting processors. The clear benefit of readout error mitigation—raising successful instances from 14 to 24 out of 40—highlights an immediate practical lesson for any near‑term experiment that seeks to explore exotic quantum dynamics beyond standard unitary evolution.

We simulate an effective change in a single qubit's inner product (IP) by implementing the channel $\mathcal{F}^η$ on a superconducting quantum processor. Whereas previous experiments simulated parity-time (PT)-symmetric dynamics with a fixed IP, this experiment implements the IP-change channel itself for metrics associated with PT-symmetric systems. Building on an earlier adversarial verification approach, we derive a process-fidelity threshold that rules out mixtures of qubit unitary operations with random discarding of runs. We test the channel for 40 metrics using a single qutrit and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. The measured fidelities exceed the threshold in 24 of 40 qutrit instances after readout error mitigation, compared with 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances. Without mitigation, 14 of 40 qutrit instances pass. These results demonstrate a direct simulation of an effective Hilbert-space IP change and its verification against a specified adversarial class, while showing the importance of readout treatment in comparing the encodings.

item.title: Rethinking Entropic Uncertainty: How measuring without a trace leads to longer keys
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by treating Alice and Bob as a single system and adding a virtual measurement register, the entropic uncertainty relation can be extended to incorporate any number of mutually unbiased bases, delivering provably tighter QKD key rates against coherent attacks. The technique not only resolves a long‑standing gap in multi‑basis security analysis but also offers a versatile tool for strengthening proofs across many quantum cryptographic and sensing protocols. As a result, future implementations that already employ multiple measurement settings can now extract longer secret keys without hardware changes, though the approach still relies on idealized virtual measurements that must be carefully mapped onto real‑world devices.

In recent years, the entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) has been one of the most prominent tools to obtain tight key rates secure against general coherent attacks for a broad class of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. Despite its success, the fundamental question of how to incorporate the statistics of more than two mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) directly into the EUR is yet to be answered. Here, we introduce a simple yet powerful shift of perspective: Instead of the usual tripartition into the systems of Alice, Bob and Eve, we treat Alice and Bob as one joint system and introduce an additional register as the third system. This register contains the results of appropriately chosen virtual measurements that leave no trace in the real branch of the protocol, but act as a conditioning on the counterfactual phase error measurements. We show that this allows us to obtain tight key rates for QKD protocols using an arbitrary number of MUBs directly and natively from the EUR. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach has a much broader relevance beyond the inclusion of multiple MUBs, allowing for improvements in many existing security proofs and the treatment of previously unexplored aspects for a wide range of protocols.

item.title: Quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures: Comparison between dispersively and directly coupled superconducting qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that superconducting transmon qubits can serve as calibrated microwave‑power sensors at millikelvin temperatures, directly comparing the performance of qubits coupled straight to a feedline versus those read out dispersively. By spanning a dynamic range from –155 dBm up to –55 dBm, the dual‑coupling device provides a practical way to measure line attenuation and drive strength—key parameters for achieving high‑fidelity gates as quantum processors scale. The approach builds on recent work integrating quantum sensors into hardware stacks, offering a simpler cryogenic metrology tool while highlighting that dispersive readout carries larger uncertainty than direct coupling. Readers should care because accurate power calibration underpins error budgeting and reproducibility across quantum computing experiments.

The Rabi frequency of a two-level system is directly proportional to the electric field amplitude being incident on this system. Taking advantage of this relationship, it is possible to use two-level systems as quantitative sensors of electric fields. Here, we apply this concept to superconducting qubits and use them for quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures. Our superconducting circuit design includes three transmon qubits directly coupled to the central microwave feedline and three transmon qubits coupled dispersively via readout resonators to the feedline. We compare both coupling schemes to assess their reliability for microwave power sensing. Further, we describe the modeling behind each power-sensing method, including an uncertainty estimation based upon repeated measurements. By combining dispersively coupled and directly coupled qubits on the same device, we are able to explore different power ranges: from $-155\;$dBm to $-130\;$dBm for the directly coupled qubits and from $-95\;$dBm to $-55\;$dBm for the dispersively coupled qubits. When determining the microwave-line attenuation for a frequency of $6.0\;$GHz from room temperature to the millikelvin stage of the cryostat, we obtain best estimates and uncertainties for the directly coupled transmons of $(74.7\pm 0.2) \;$dB and for the dispersively coupled transmons of $(75.4\pm 6.8) \;$dB. The larger uncertainty of the dispersively coupled qubit measurements indicates that these qubits are less reliable for power sensing than the directly coupled qubits, most likely, due to the additional coupling resonator, whose transfer function is difficult to estimate accurately. Our results constitute the first step towards validation of qubit power sensing in dilution fridges, leading towards traceability for cryogenic microwave measurements.

item.title: Sequential strategy for depolarizing strength estimation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that repeatedly feeding the same probe through a depolarizing channel can linearly boost the quantum Fisher information for very low noise and even let a single‑qubit probe outperform optimal two‑qubit schemes once three or more repetitions are used, highlighting a surprisingly simple route to sharper noise‑parameter estimates. By identifying an optimal finite number of channel applications in the weak‑noise regime, the work connects directly to current efforts to calibrate and mitigate errors on NISQ hardware where precise depolarizing‑strength knowledge is essential for error‑correction thresholds and quantum sensing protocols. The results suggest that sequential encoding—already easy to implement on existing platforms—could become a practical tool for faster, more accurate characterization of noisy channels without the overhead of entangled multi‑qubit probes.

We study the advantages of applying a sequential strategy for enhancing the precision in estimating the strength $p$ of a depolarizing channel, using qudit and two-qubit probes. The sequential strategy requires that the same depolarizing channel is repeatedly applied $M$ times to the quantum probe. From the analysis of the probe's output state, both the quantum Fisher information (QFI) and its regularization RQFI, given from multiplication by $p$, are analyzed. We determine that in the limit of $p \to 0$, the QFI is {\it linearly amplified} with the number of channel repetitions. Instead, in the weak-noise regime, the QFI is maximized at a finite value of $M$. Then, the RQFI decreases more quickly with $p$ as $M$ increases. In particular, for two-qubit probes, the RQFI decreases with the depolarization strength proportionally to the amount of correlation between the qubits. The greater the number of channel repetitions, the wider the range of $p$ for which the initial state of the probe that allows for the maximization of the QFI is a separable state. We also show that a single qubit probe undergoing a sequential encoding protocol outperforms the optimal two-qubit single-round QFI for $M>3$ in the weak-noise regime.

item.title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces SCOPE, a compiler that uses an operator‑Schmidt time surrogate to steer pulse‑level optimization toward the shortest possible execution latency, directly addressing the coherence‑time bottleneck that limits near‑term quantum processors. By integrating a physics‑based lower bound on nonlocal evolution into a genetic search, SCOPE achieves up to a two‑fold reduction in critical‑path duration compared with the previous EPOC framework across a range of benchmark circuits, including a six‑qubit QFT. The results demonstrate that latency‑aware compilation can translate into tangible speedups without increasing gate count, highlighting a practical pathway for squeezing more algorithmic depth out of noisy hardware. However, the approach depends on accurate coupling models and incurs extra classical optimization overhead, so its benefits will be most pronounced when pulse‑level control is already available on the target device.

Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

item.title: What kind of quantum advantage is this?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a growing source of confusion in the field by offering a clear taxonomy that separates the underlying mechanisms—structural, interference‑based, and coherent—from how essential they are for achieving a genuine quantum advantage. By formalising a diagnostic framework and an entanglement‑breaking test, it gives researchers a practical tool to evaluate new algorithmic claims against the strongest classical adversaries, something that has been missing amid recent “quantum supremacy” debates. The approach also clarifies why certain problems like the hidden subgroup case demand cross‑copy coherence, helping the community focus effort on truly novel quantum resources rather than superficial speedups.

Quantum advantage encompasses fundamentally different claims, from resource reductions to exponential separations in sample complexity. Evaluating these claims requires distinguishing how an algorithm achieves an advantage from what is necessary for the separation and how strongly it is supported against classical alternatives. We propose a multi-label taxonomy that makes these distinctions explicit, classifying structural, interference, and coherent mechanisms while separately recording their necessity and the evidence for the classical comparison. Coherent mechanisms are further divided into memory and output, reflecting distinct restrictions on quantum information processing. A two-part entanglement-breaking test distinguishes loss of information from loss of algorithmic efficiency. The hidden subgroup problem illustrates the distinction: among the cases examined, cross-copy coherence is information-theoretically necessary only for the symmetric group. We present this as a diagnostic methodology rather than a theory of quantum advantage: for a new claim, it identifies the relevant adversary, separates the mechanisms a protocol uses from those shown to be necessary, and records the strength of the evidence and the quality of the advantage separately.
